newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Research Alert-Salomon downgrades Telecom.
newsitem.headline: Research Alert-Salomon downgrades Telecom.

text.p: Salomon Brothers Asia-Pacific said on Tuesday it was downgrading its recommendation on Telecom Corp of New Zealand shares to hold from buy "because the upturn in the company's business appears to be moving further into the future".
A slow economy for the next nine months, plus potentially stiffer competition, will put a dampener on revenue growth, the investment house said in a report.
At the same time, spending on Telecom New Zealand's cable venture First Media was likely to keep cost growth running in the high single digits, Salomon said.
"This combination means at least another year of slow profit growth," it said.
Salomon noted that in the March year the New Zealand economy grew by 1.8 percent, less than a third of its growth rate two years earlier.
That, together with continued competition, meant Telecom had revenue growth of 0.9 percent on long distance calls, 4.3 percent on international calls and 5.8 percent on cellular.
All these growth numbers were less than a quarter of the year before, it pointed out.
Meanwhile operating expenses grew by 9.6 percent for the year against 3.3 percent last year. Much of those increases came from the establishment of First Media and the XTRA internet service.
"If anything, these costs will be even more difficult to control over the next year, as the company continues spending on its cable venture," Salomon said.
Salomon said that over the last nine months Telecom had done well to increase its overall market share to 82 percent from 78 percent against fast-growing rival Clear Communications.
But it warned the recent resignation of Clear chief executive Andrew Makin may result in reinvigorated competition.

The report took issue with some commentators who have said that New Zealand has a growth trajectory of its own which could make it, and shares like Telecom, a safe haven for investors in the event of a downturn in the U.S. economy.

Salomon argued that past experience showed that if the U.S. economy did indeed go into recession then New Zealand would follow within a fairly short space of time and it would probably be a good time to leave the market rather than to enter it.
